title: Episode 307: Richard III: The Princes in the Tower, Bosworth Field, and the Last Plantagenet

The electrifying, controversial life of King Richard III, the last Plantagenet monarch of England. Loyal brother and brilliant northern administrator under Edward IV, Richard seized power in a breathtaking coup following Edward's sudden death in 1483, declaring the young princes illegitimate and claiming the throne. When twelve-year-old Edward V and his brother vanished forever inside the dark walls of the Tower of London, Richard's reign was consumed by suspicion and rebellion. At the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485, Richard died fighting with desperate gallantry, shouting for the crown. In 2012, his battle-scarred skeleton was unearthed beneath a Leicester car park. Discover the last Plantagenet.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the most debated, vilified, and tragic monarch in British history: the king immortalized by Shakespeare as a hunchbacked monster, whose true face and fallen bones were finally revealed five centuries later: King Richard III. Here is George with the extraordinary saga of the last Plantagenet.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: LOYALTY BINDS ME: THE NORTHERN LORDSHIP: 1452 TO 1483
Born in October 1452 at Fotheringhay Castle in Northamptonshire, Richard was the eleventh and youngest child of Richard, Duke of York. Slight of build and quiet by temperament, Richard spent his adolescence in the household of Warwick the Kingmaker at Middleham Castle in Wensleydale. Unlike his treacherous brother Clarence, Richard was fiercely, unshakeably loyal to his eldest brother King Edward IV, adopting as his personal motto 'Loyaulte me lie'—'Loyalty binds me.' He shared Edward's bitter exile in Flanders and fought with conspicuous bravery commanding the vanguard at Barnet and Tewkesbury when he was barely eighteen years old. Rewarded with Warwick's vast northern estates and marrying Warwick's younger daughter, Anne Neville, Richard served for a decade as the Lord of the North. From his stronghold at Middleham, Richard governed Yorkshire, Durham, and the Scottish Marches with exemplary justice, fairness, and administrative efficiency, earning the deep and abiding adoration of northern Englishmen. In 1482, he commanded a victorious royal army into Scotland, capturing Edinburgh and securing the border fortress of Berwick-upon-Tweed for the English Crown. To all of England, Richard of Gloucester appeared the very model of chivalric probity, martial vigor, and unblemished loyalty. Richard's decade as Lord of the North was characterized by an extraordinary devotion to impartial justice and fair dealing for ordinary folk. From his seat at Middleham, he established the Council of the North, ensuring that northern commoners could seek legal redress against predatory magnates without traveling three hundred miles to Westminster. The city of York held him in such deep reverence that its municipal records referred to him with genuine affection as their 'most noble protector', a bond of mutual loyalty that remained unbroken even after his catastrophic fall at Bosworth.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE STONY STRATFORD COUP: APRIL 1483
When King Edward IV died suddenly in April 1483, the twelve-year-old Prince of Wales was residing at Ludlow Castle in Shropshire under the tutelage of his maternal uncle, Anthony Woodville, Earl Rivers. The Woodvilles moved swiftly to seize total control of the boy king, aiming to escort him to London with a private army of two thousand men and crown him immediately, effectively freezing Gloucester out of the regency. Richard was warned by Lord Hastings, the Lord Chamberlain in London, that his life was in mortal danger. On April 30, 1483, Richard intercepted Rivers and the young king's entourage at Stony Stratford in Buckinghamshire. After dining cordially with Rivers that evening, Richard struck with lightning precision at dawn: he arrested Earl Rivers, Sir Richard Grey, and royal chamberlain Thomas Vaughan, sending them north under armed guard to be imprisoned at Pontefract Castle. Approaching the terrified twelve-year-old Edward V, Richard dropped to one knee, kissed his nephew's hand, and swore that he had acted only to save the king from traitors. In London, when Queen Elizabeth Woodville learned of the coup, she fled in blind panic into the sanctuary of Westminster Abbey with her younger son, nine-year-old Richard of Shrewsbury, and her daughters, taking with her the royal plate and jewels. Anthony Woodville, Earl Rivers, was one of the most cultured men in England, the translator of Dictes and Sayings of the Philosophers and William Caxton's chief patron. Yet Richard understood that Rivers' possession of the boy king gave the Woodville faction an unassailable weapon. When Richard confronted Rivers at Stony Stratford, he pointedly accused the Woodvilles of seeking to monopolize the royal person, dispossess the king's paternal uncles, and govern through private ambition rather than royal council. Rivers was taken to Pontefract, where he wrote a poignant last poem before his execution.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE TOWER, HASTINGS' EXECUTION, AND TITULUS REGIUS: JUNE 1483
Arriving in London on May 4, Richard escorted young Edward V into the city clad in blue velvet, lodging the boy in the royal apartments of the Tower of London—the traditional residence of English monarchs prior to their coronations. On June 13, at a council meeting inside the Tower, a terrifying drama unfolded. Richard suddenly accused Lord Hastings of plotting with Queen Elizabeth and Jane Shore against his life, slamming his fist on the table. Armed men burst into the chamber; Hastings was dragged down into the courtyard and summarily beheaded upon a log of construction timber without trial. Days later, Richard coerced the Archbishop of Canterbury into persuading the queen to release nine-year-old Prince Richard from sanctuary to join his brother in the Tower. Then came the ideological bombshell: on June 22, at St. Paul's Cross, the preacher Dr. Ralph Shaa delivered a sensational sermon announcing that Edward IV had entered into a binding pre-contract of marriage with Lady Eleanor Talbot before his secret wedding to Elizabeth Woodville. Under canon law, this rendered the marriage bigamous and all of Edward's children illegitimate bastards. On June 26, Parliament formally petitioned Richard to accept the crown, codified in the statute Titulus Regius. On July 6, 1483, Richard III and Anne Neville were crowned at Westminster Abbey. The sudden execution of Lord Hastings on June 13 remains one of the most chilling scenes in English history: Richard bared his arm in the council chamber, alleging it was withered by Jane Shore's sorcery, though courtiers knew it had been slender since his youth. Hastings was hurried onto the Tower green, denied a trial or spiritual counsel, and beheaded upon a rough-hewn log. The pre-contract defense, advanced by Bishop Stillington of Bath and Wells, was legally credible under canon law: an unsolemnized pre-contract between consenting adults constituted a valid, binding marriage, nullifying any subsequent union.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE PRINCES IN THE TOWER: MYSTERY AND DISAPPEARANCE: 1483
Following the glittering coronation, the fate of the two young princes in the Tower became the darkest and most enduring mystery in English history. In the summer of 1483, Italian traveler Dominic Mancini recorded that twelve-year-old Edward V and his brother were seen less and less behind the barred windows of the Garden Tower—later named the Bloody Tower—shooting arrows and playing in the courtyard, until finally they ceased to appear altogether. Mancini noted that young Edward, believing his death was imminent, made daily confessions and spent his hours in prayer. Rumors swept London and the courts of Europe that the boys had been murdered. Sir Thomas More, writing three decades later during the Tudor reign, claimed that Richard dispatched his loyal master of the horse, Sir James Tyrrell, who instructed two assassins, Miles Forest and John Dighton, to smother the sleeping princes beneath feather pillows before burying them at the foot of the White Tower staircase. While modern historians debate whether the murder was ordered by Richard, his henchman the Duke of Buckingham, or later by Henry VII, Richard never produced the living boys to quell the rumors. In 1674, workmen renovating the White Tower unearthed a wooden chest containing the skeletons of two children, which Charles II interred in Westminster Abbey as the murdered princes. During his sole parliament in January 1484, Richard enacted some of the most enlightened, progressive legislation in medieval English legal history. He abolished the hated 'benevolences'—forced arbitrary loans extracted by Edward IV—instituted a system of bail for accused persons awaiting trial, mandated that jurors be men of substance and integrity to prevent bribed verdicts, and ordered all laws to be written in English rather than French or Latin so common citizens could understand their rights. Yet these visionary legal reforms were overshadowed by the haunting, silent absence of the two boys in the Tower.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: BUCKINGHAM'S REBELLION AND PERSONAL TRAGEDY: 1483 TO 1484
The disappearance of the princes destroyed Richard's political moral authority. In October 1483, barely three months into his reign, a widespread rebellion exploded across southern England. Astonishingly, the insurrection was led by Henry Stafford, Duke of Buckingham—the very man who had helped Richard seize the throne. Buckingham allied with the exiled Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, the last surviving Lancastrian claimant residing in Brittany, proposing that Tudor marry Edward IV's eldest daughter, Elizabeth of York, to unite the rival factions. The rebellion was foiled by torrential autumn rains and floods of the River Severn—remembered as 'Buckingham's Water'—which prevented Buckingham's Welsh army from crossing. Buckingham was captured, dragged to Salisbury marketplace, and beheaded without trial. But personal grief soon struck Richard's household with devastating force: in April 1484, his only legitimate child, ten-year-old Edward of Middleham, died suddenly of fever, leaving the king and queen in inconsolable sorrow. Less than a year later, in March 1485, Queen Anne Neville died of tuberculosis. Desperately isolated, surrounded by whispers that he intended to marry his own niece Elizabeth of York, Richard watched his political support crumble as noblemen defected across the English Channel to join Henry Tudor's growing court in exile. The death of his son Edward of Middleham at Middleham Castle broke Richard's heart; contemporary records describe the king and Queen Anne as nearly driven insane with sudden grief. Richard named his nephew John de la Pole, Earl of Lincoln, as his provisional heir, but the death of Queen Anne in March 1485 sparked malicious court gossip that Richard had poisoned his wife to marry his niece Elizabeth of York. Richard was forced to summon the mayor and aldermen of London to the Great Hall of St. John's at Clerkenwell to publicly deny the foul rumors, weeping before the assembly as he proclaimed his innocence.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE BATTLE OF BOSWORTH FIELD: AUGUST 22, 1485
On August 7, 1485, Henry Tudor landed at Mill Bay in Pembrokeshire with two thousand French and Scottish mercenaries and Lancastrian exiles, marching through Wales under the Red Dragon banner of Cadwaladr to rally his countrymen. On August 22, Richard intercepted Tudor's army near Market Bosworth in Leicestershire. Richard held the high ground atop Ambion Hill with ten thousand men, outnumbering Tudor's five thousand. But the battle was decided by treachery. Standing aloof on the flank was Lord Stanley with six thousand men, waiting to see which side would gain the advantage. When Richard ordered the Earl of Northumberland to advance his northern division, Northumberland refused to move. Realizing his commanders were betraying him and seeing Henry Tudor isolated with a small bodyguard in the valley below, Richard decided to settle the crown of England with his own broadsword. Wearing a golden circlet atop his helmet and surrounded by eighty trusted knights, Richard spurred his magnificent white courser down Ambion Hill in a thunderous, desperate cavalry charge. He cut down Tudor's giant standard-bearer, Sir William Brandon, unhorsed Sir John Cheyne, and traded sword blows mere yards from Tudor himself. At that fateful second, Lord Stanley ordered his men to charge, slamming into Richard's flank. Surrounded, unhorsed, and fighting like a lion in the bog, Richard shouted, 'Treason! Treason!' as he was struck down by halberd blows to the skull. The last Plantagenet king was dead. Richard spent the eve of Bosworth at Leicester, staying at the Blue Boar Inn, where his portable carved oak bedstead contained a secret false bottom filled with gold coins. Chroniclers recorded that on the night before the battle, Richard was tormented by terrifying nightmares in which demons dragged him down into the abyss. At dawn, he appeared pale and haggard, but his warrior courage never wavered: when urged to flee the field on a fresh courser as the lines collapsed, Richard fiercely refused, shouting: 'God forbid that I yield one step! This day I will die as King of England, or I will win!'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE KING BENEATH THE CAR PARK: LEICESTER 2012
Following the battle, Richard's battered, naked corpse was tied across the back of a horse, paraded through Leicester to prove he was dead, and hastily buried without ceremony in the choir of the church of the Greyfriars friary. When Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries in 1538, the friary was demolished, and Richard's grave was lost to memory, with legend claiming his bones had been thrown into the River Soar. But in August 2012, an extraordinary archaeological excavation led by the University of Leicester and the Richard III Society dug trenches in a Leicester city council parking lot. On the very first day of digging, excavators uncovered a skeleton bearing severe scoliosis—a curvature of the spine—and eleven battle injuries, including eight devastating trauma wounds to the skull inflicted by swords and halberds. Radiocarbon dating, osteological analysis, and revolutionary mitochondrial DNA testing matched the skeleton directly to living maternal descendants of Richard's sister, Anne of York. The discovery confirmed that while Richard had a curved spine, he was no withered monster, but a fierce, agile warrior king. In March 2015, five centuries after his violent death, King Richard III was reinterred with full royal dignity and solemn Christian rites inside Leicester Cathedral, resting finally under a tomb of Swaledale fossil stone. The 2012 discovery of Richard's remains beneath the 'R' painted on the asphalt of the Leicester council car park solved centuries of historical mystery. Forensic CT scans revealed that the fatal blow was a deep halberd cut to the base of the skull, shearing away the bone and exposing the brain. The osteological reconstruction proved that while he suffered from adolescent scoliosis, his right shoulder was merely slightly elevated, readily concealed beneath tailored doublet coats. His reburial in Leicester Cathedral in 2015, attended by thousands, closed the bloody medieval chapter of the Wars of the Roses with peace and solemn prayer.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for joining us for this episode of Most Fascinating Stories. If you enjoyed this chapter of Richard III: The Princes in the Tower, Bosworth Field, and the Last Plantagenet, subscribe to the show, share it with a fellow history lover, and tune in next Tuesday for our next journey into history's most extraordinary events. Until next time, I'm Rebecca.
